subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 72-year-old woman is hospitalized with an inferior myocardial infarction. On hospital day 4 she develops acute pulmonary edema. Auscultation reveals a new holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla. She is tachycardic and hypotensive.
question: Which of the following complications of myocardial infarction is most likely responsible for this patient's findings?

options.text: Free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
Papillary muscle rupture causing mitral regurgitation
True ventricular aneurysm formation
Interventricular septal rupture with left-to-right shunt
Postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis

explanation_correct: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 3-14 days after infarction and causes acute severe mitral regurgitation, producing a new holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla with flash pulmonary edema. It is one of the macrophage-era mechanical complications that arise while the infarct is centrally yellow-brown and soft.

explanation_incorrect.A: Free wall rupture in the 3-14 day window causes hemopericardium and tamponade (hypotension with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds), not a new apical holosystolic murmur with pulmonary edema.
explanation_incorrect.C: A true ventricular aneurysm is a late complication (2 weeks to several months) with a risk of mural thrombus; it produces persistent heart failure and arrhythmias, not abrupt day-4 pulmonary edema with a new murmur.
explanation_incorrect.D: Interventricular septal rupture causes a left-to-right shunt with a harsh murmur and a step-up in oxygen saturation at the right ventricle; the murmur described here is apical and radiates to the axilla, the classic location of mitral regurgitation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis occurs at 1-3 days and causes pleuritic chest pain with a pericardial friction rub, not acute heart failure with a holosystolic murmur.

educationalObjective: Mechanical ruptures (free wall, papillary muscle, septum) occur 3-14 days post-MI during macrophage-mediated softening; papillary muscle rupture presents with acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 59-year-old man receives fibrinolytic therapy 90 minutes after the onset of an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Coronary flow is restored, but the subsequent ventricular dysfunction is worse than anticipated. Histologic examination of the affected myocardium shows hypercontraction of myofibrils with dark eosinophilic stripes.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this histologic finding after reperfusion?

options.text: Acute inflammation with neutrophils surrounding the infarct
Macrophage-mediated structural degradation of necrotic myocardium
Granulation tissue formation at the margins of the infarct
Deposition of collagen forming a contracted gray-white scar
Free radical generation and increased Ca2+ influx causing hypercontraction of myofibrils

explanation_correct: Reperfusion injury after restoring coronary flow generates free radicals and increased Ca2+ influx, causing hypercontraction of myofibrils seen as dark eosinophilic stripes (contraction bands). This is a recognized consequence of reperfusion within the 0-24 hour phase, alongside the release of cell contents into the blood.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute inflammation with neutrophils characterizes the infarct at 1-3 days and reflects the response to coagulative necrosis, not the myofibrillar hypercontraction of reperfusion injury.
explanation_incorrect.B: Macrophage-mediated structural degradation occurs at 3-14 days and explains the central yellow-brown softening that predisposes to mechanical ruptures, not contraction-band necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Granulation tissue appears at the margins of the infarct at 3-14 days as part of healing, not within reperfused myofibers as eosinophilic stripes.
explanation_incorrect.D: A contracted gray-white scar forms from 2 weeks to several months and represents completed repair by fibrosis, an entirely different stage of infarct evolution.

educationalObjective: Reperfusion injury produces free radicals and increased Ca2+ influx with hypercontracted myofibrils (dark eosinophilic stripes/contraction bands).

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 68-year-old man suffered a large anterior myocardial infarction 6 days ago. He suddenly becomes hypotensive and unresponsive. Examination shows distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, and echocardiography demonstrates blood in the pericardial space compressing the right ventricle.
question: Which of the following best explains why this complication typically occurs at this point in infarct evolution?

options.text: Macrophage infiltration of the infarct with central yellow-brown softening of the necrotic myocardium
Wavy fibers and early coagulative necrosis in the first hours of the infarct
Extensive coagulative necrosis with surrounding acute neutrophilic inflammation
Complete formation of a contracted gray-white scar with collagen deposition
Hypercontraction of myofibrils with dark eosinophilic stripes after reperfusion

explanation_correct: At 3-14 days the infarct shows a hyperemic border with central yellow-brown softening, and histology shows macrophages (then granulation tissue) clearing necrotic myocardium. This macrophage-mediated weakening of the free wall predisposes to rupture at this time, which causes hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade — exactly this patient's hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds.

explanation_incorrect.B: Wavy fibers (0-4 hours) and early coagulative necrosis (4-24 hours) mark the first day, when the myocardium is not yet softened enough to rupture.
explanation_incorrect.C: Extensive coagulative necrosis with neutrophilic acute inflammation is the 1-3 day phase, associated with fibrinous pericarditis rather than free wall rupture.
explanation_incorrect.D: The contracted gray-white scar of 2 weeks to several months is strong fibrous tissue; rupture risk has passed by then, though a true aneurysm may form instead.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypercontraction bands reflect reperfusion injury to myofibrils in the first 24 hours and do not weaken the ventricular wall enough to cause day-6 rupture.

educationalObjective: Free wall rupture causing tamponade is a 3-14 day complication explained by macrophage-mediated clearing and central softening of necrotic myocardium.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 70-year-old man is evaluated 6 weeks after a large anterior myocardial infarction for worsening exertional dyspnea and two episodes of transient left hand weakness. ECG shows persistent ST-segment elevation in V1-V4. Echocardiogram demonstrates dyskinetic bulging of the left ventricular apex during systole and a layered filling defect within the dilated apical segment.
question: Which of the following complications of myocardial infarction best explains this patient's presentation?

options.text: Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm contained by pericardium with a high risk of rupture
Postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis with pericardial effusion
Interventricular septal rupture causing a left-to-right shunt
True ventricular aneurysm with mural thrombus formation
Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation

explanation_correct: A true ventricular aneurysm is a 2-weeks-to-several-months complication of a large transmural infarct: the healed, thinned scar bulges dyskinetically, classically with persistent ST-segment elevation. Its key risk is mural thrombus formation within the aneurysm, which can embolize and cause systemic events such as stroke — explaining the transient left hand weakness.

explanation_incorrect.A: A pseudoaneurysm results from a contained free wall rupture during the 3-14 day window and its defining risk is rupture into the pericardium; a chronic, scar-lined apical bulge 6 weeks out with mural thrombus is a true aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.B: Postinfarction fibrinous pericarditis occurs at 1-3 days with pleuritic pain and a friction rub, and the postcardiac injury syndrome is also an early-late pericardial process; neither produces an apical dyskinetic bulge with mural thrombus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Septal rupture occurs at 3-14 days from macrophage-mediated structural degradation and creates an acute left-to-right shunt with hemodynamic collapse, not a chronic apical bulge.
explanation_incorrect.E: Papillary muscle rupture is a 3-14 day complication causing acute severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema, incompatible with a stable 6-week course.

educationalObjective: A true ventricular aneurysm (2 weeks to several months post-MI) shows persistent ST elevation and carries a risk of mural thrombus with systemic embolization; pseudoaneurysm (3-14 days) risks rupture.
